children: By Heather Gillers and Margot Patrick
Trinidad Navarro had been in his job as Delaware's insurance commissioner barely a year when Mark Walter's companies threatened to leave the state.

The regulator's financial examination of Walter's Clear Spring Life had so displeased the billionaire investor and his executives that they said in 2018 they might relocate the insurer and its sister company, Delaware Life, people familiar with the matter said. The decision, the department knew, would mean losing Delaware's third-largest insurer.

Navarro's department moved to smooth things over with Walter's companies, which stayed put and received a clean bill of health in subsequent state examinations, most recently in 2023. But by 2025, the two insurers' portfolios had filled up with tens of billions of dollars in loans to other entities tied to Walter — investments that the insurers later acknowledged weren't properly reported as insider deals.

Those loans, and whether Walter hid their connections to affiliated entities, are the subject of investigations by federal authorities. Delaware's insurance regulator now says it didn't know the insider investments were sitting on the insurers' books because it was "intentionally misled" through "a hidden scheme" that it said also deceived outside auditors, ratings firms and the insurance companies themselves.

Navarro's department told The Wall Street Journal it is also conducting its own investigation. It didn't say how it reached its conclusion about the alleged deception, or who it thinks carried it out.

The federal probes into Walter's undisclosed loans have turned Delaware's elected insurance commissioner into a lightning rod in a debate that is playing out across the country: whether state regulators are up to the task of overseeing the cadre of sophisticated Wall Street players that have poured private assets into insurance portfolios.

Critics and watchdogs say the limitations of overstretched and underfunded state regulators are part of what made those insurers such juicy takeover targets in the first place. Some in the industry joke that NAIC — the acronym for the standard-setting body of state regulators, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners — stands for "No Action Immediately Contemplated."

The NAIC said in a statement that in recent years state regulators "have strengthened investment oversight, enhanced disclosure requirements, increased scrutiny of complex and privately structured assets, and updated capital frameworks to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market. In fact, many of these actions generated substantial industry pushback."

On Thursday, in its first detailed statement on the scandal that has enveloped Walter's businesses, Navarro's department disputed the assertion that state regulators "should have been aware of this deception," an idea it said is based on "misidentified fragments of misstated information." The department said some of the borrowers who received loans placed in insurer portfolios "later transferred those obligations and investments to affiliates of their parent entities. In many cases the affiliated entities are controlled by Mark Walter."

The regulator said it was in the dark about the extent of those affiliated loans. Then this past summer Delaware Life and Clear Spring said it had been subpoenaed in February by federal authorities and was revising its tally of affiliated deals to a combined $24 billion from around $1 billion.

However, the Journal found that Navarro's office for years had clues that Walter's companies were operating outside of norms, according to regulatory filings, department documents and interviews with people familiar with the matter. It knew of a program specifically designed to let Walter and his business associates borrow from the insurance companies, and that many of those investments weren't classified as affiliated, according to people familiar with the matter. In less than a decade, that lending grew from a couple of billion dollars to one third or more of the insurers' assets, an analysis by the Journal found.

The Delaware insurance department declined to answer questions about that program but noted that Delaware Life's financial reports — the same ones that vastly understated the firm's affiliated assets — were "audited by a major international accounting firm."

Walter's holding company, TWG Global, has said there is no fraud and no victims. Group 1001, the TWG business that owns the insurers, has said it found errors in how it identified and reported related-party investments and would strengthen its governance and financial controls. The insurers are now in the process of cutting their exposure. Delaware Life on Monday said it scaled back affiliated assets to 35% as of mid-November, from 42% at the end of 2025.

"TWG respects the Delaware Department of Insurance and is cooperating with the Department and other governmental authorities," a TWG spokesman said in a statement. "We strongly disagree with any suggestion that TWG misled anyone. Because these matters are under review, we will address them through the appropriate process."
A spokesman for Group 1001 declined to comment.
News of the federal probe over the summer rocked the financial world and set off calls for reforms to the state insurance regulation system.

"If the regulators don't know how many affiliated transactions are in the investment portfolios of these life insurers, that's worrisome to me and it tells me that they need to demand more transparency of the insurers licensed in their state," said Doug Heller, director of insurance at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. "We can't hope that a federal prosecutor is going to come in and clean up."

At an investor conference in September, Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan, whose firm operates the nation's biggest seller of annuities, piled on, blasting the Delaware department for not spotting the problems.
Ex-cop on the beat

A former police officer and county sheriff, Navarro was elected commissioner a decade ago after pledging to keep down bills for health and car insurance. He is one of 11 elected state insurance commissioners, and responsible for supervising more than half a trillion dollars in insurer investments, the fifth-most of any state, according to data from AM Best. Yet his department's budget, at $31 million, ranked 20th in 2024, the most recent year for which the National Association of Insurance Commissioners reported data.

To sell insurance, companies must be financially sound so that they can attract customers and pay out policies years into the future. State officials act as consumer watchdogs and financial auditors, monitoring and enforcing rules around marketing, pricing, governance and investments.

In practice, an often-shoestring staff ends up juggling all of those responsibilities while also promoting the state for business. Insurers can be domiciled in — and therefore regulated by — one state but have their headquarters hundreds of miles away. Delaware Life is based in Zionsville, Ind., while its chief investment officer and some other staff are in a Boston suburb.
Like other state insurance departments, Delaware leans on outside help to handle most of the details behind auditing company balance sheets and checking solvency.
Before assuming the post, Navarro's insurance experience was limited to two years in his 20s when he worked as a life-insurance agent before joining the New Castle County Sheriff's Department.

As commissioner, Navarro championed legislation to shore up Delaware's place as a destination for "captives" — in-house reinsurers that allow life insurers to hold less capital. Delaware had the third most such companies of any state in 2025, according to the Insurance Information Institute. Indeed, Delaware's hospitality toward captives helped make another local life insurer, Brighthouse, an attractive target for a company run by one of Walter's former colleagues. Navarro has yet to rule on the merger more than a year after it was announced.

The Delaware native's decade as commissioner spanned a shift in the life insurance industry. Private-equity firms and alternative asset managers scooped up companies and books of business to add fee-generating assets. They moved insurers out of traditional corporate bonds and into higher-yielding private credit, stepping through loopholes that let esoteric private investments count as safer than a blue-chip for capital.

Century-old state insurance laws couldn't keep up with all the financial optimization. The NAIC had to redefine basic concepts — like what constitutes a bond, or who is a related party — to try to stop the rule bending.

The risks weren't theoretical. In 2019, The Journal reported that North Carolina entrepreneur Greg Lindberg diverted $2 billion from his insurance group to buy companies, homes, a jet and a yacht, by borrowing through more than 100 companies issuing private-credit loans and bonds to the insurers. He was sentenced to 12 years prison this year for fraud and bribery; his companies still owe thousands of policyholders more than $1 billion.
Walter's private market moves

Walter is the CEO of Guggenheim Partners, a midsize investment management and securities firm he co-founded in the late 1990s. He was known to few outside Wall Street until his investment group's glitzy purchase of the Los Angeles Dodgers raised his profile — and led to other trophy purchases and prominent roles in arts and philanthropy.

He and some of his business partners also assembled a stable of insurance companies after the 2008-09 financial crisis, when regulators were eager for savvy financial firms to take on insurers still reeling from the downturn. Central to Walter's pitch: the case that higher-yielding private debt would improve the returns of insurers that had until then rarely strayed from plain-vanilla bond investments.
Clear Spring, initially controlled by Guggenheim Partners, redomiciled in Delaware from Iowa in 2010. Walter and some associates bought Delaware Life in 2013.

In a financial exam of Clear Spring, then called Guggenheim Life, for the year ending in 2015, Delaware examiners found a raft of issues, detailed in a public report in October 2017. Those included a breach of investment-concentration limits in a set of separate accounts, whose policyholders included Walter, according to people familiar with the matter. The assets held there included slices of his trophy asset the Dodgers.
A $552 million loan Clear Spring extended to leverage the investments posed additional risks, the examiners found, and recommended reducing it.

The exam findings set off a series of meetings with department officials and Walter's staff, who found the wording too strong, according to people familiar with the matter. There was talk of leaving the state. Walter's staff successfully pushed for a watered-down version in a management letter that would be accessible to other state regulators, a person familiar with the matter said.
A spokesman for Group 1001 said the companies at one point discussed with regulators relocating to Illinois, but didn't make a threat.

Navarro's department also allowed an unconventional borrowing program by Walter at the two insurers to balloon, according to some of the people. In November 2018, the Journal reported on a program called Safe Harbor, though which Walter and some associates had borrowed billions of dollars from the insurers for their outside business interests, which a lawyer for Walter said didn't present any conflicts of interest because Walter and the associates had pledged back personal assets to financially support the insurers if needed.

The CEO of Delaware Life and Clear Spring, Dan Towriss, visited Dover the next month to give the department more details, people familiar with the matter said. In 2020, the Journal reported that the insurance financing for Walter and his associates' investments had grown to at least $10 billion.

After Walter's two insurers reclassified almost half their investments as affiliated this past summer, people from Walter's insurance group told the Delaware department and ratings firms that they hadn't known the proceeds from dozens of private-credit loans and bonds were going to Walter's companies.

"Upon identifying the issue, we owned it, disclosed it, and took immediate steps to address it," Group 1001 said in September. This week, Delaware Life said it is taking steps to improve governance and identify potential conflicts of interest in its lending.

The commissioner's office said in its Thursday statement that assertions that it could or should have been aware of the extent of Walter's insurers' affiliated investments are based on a "drumbeat of inaccuracies."

"The regurgitation of falsehoods now threatens to harm the public and the department is issuing this statement to urge caution in relying on these unfounded speculations and reports," Navarro's office said.

Meanwhile, policyholders who own Delaware Life and Clear Spring annuities have sued Walter and the insurers for failing to disclose the extent of their affiliated investments. Ratings firms have revised their outlook for Delaware Life to negative.
